clinicalPearls: An X-linked dominant chondrodysplasia punctata caused by mutations in EBP, which encodes emopamil-binding protein (a sterol isomerase in cholesterol biosynthesis)
Because it is X-linked dominant, it is usually seen in females and is typically lethal in most affected males, with survivors often mosaic
Features follow a mosaic distribution along the lines of Blaschko, producing patchy skin changes (early ichthyosiform erythroderma, later follicular atrophoderma and patchy alopecia)

Skeletal features include asymmetric limb shortening (rhizomelic or otherwise), scoliosis and the characteristic punctate (stippled) epiphyseal calcification (chondrodysplasia punctata) seen on infant radiographs
Cataracts, often asymmetric or sectorial, are a common and important association
The stippled epiphyses tend to disappear after infancy, so early imaging is more informative
A key differential is a phenocopy from maternal warfarin exposure in pregnancy, so a medication history is essential
Diagnosis is supported by a characteristic sterol profile (raised 8-dehydrocholesterol and 8(9)-cholestenol) and confirmed by EBP testing
reference.pathophysiology: Conradi-Hunermann syndrome is caused by mutations in EBP, encoding emopamil-binding protein, an enzyme (sterol delta-8, delta-7 isomerase) acting late in cholesterol biosynthesis. Loss of enzyme activity leads to accumulation of abnormal sterol precursors and a relative deficiency of cholesterol in developing tissues, disturbing sterol-dependent developmental signalling and cartilage and skin development. Because the gene is X-linked and the trait behaves as dominant, random X-inactivation in females produces the mosaic, Blaschko-line pattern of skin and skeletal involvement, while non-mosaic affected males usually do not survive.
additionalDifferentials: Warfarin embryopathy (medication phenocopy with stippled epiphyses)
Vitamin K epoxide reductase / maternal vitamin K deficiency effects
Other congenital ichthyoses with skeletal change
additionalInvestigations: Plasma sterol analysis showing raised 8-dehydrocholesterol and 8(9)-cholestenol
Molecular testing of EBP to confirm the diagnosis
Infant skeletal radiographs to capture stippled (punctate) epiphyseal calcification before it resolves
Spinal imaging to assess scoliosis and asymmetry
Detailed maternal medication history to exclude a warfarin phenocopy
redFlags: Dense or progressive cataracts threatening vision in infancy
Rapidly progressive scoliosis requiring orthopaedic intervention
Severe neonatal skin involvement with barrier compromise
An affected male, prompting evaluation for mosaicism and a guarded prognosis
reference.prognosis: Affected females usually survive with variable orthopaedic, ophthalmological and dermatological problems and generally normal cognition, whereas the non-mosaic male phenotype is typically severe or lethal; long-term care focuses on scoliosis, cataracts and skin.
pitfalls: Missing a warfarin-exposure phenocopy through inadequate medication history
Delaying radiographs so that transient stippled epiphyses are no longer visible
Overlooking asymmetric cataracts that need timely ophthalmic treatment
Assuming autosomal recessive rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata and mismanaging counselling
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Manage the skin manifestations with emollients and topical keratolytic or moisturising therapy for ichthyosiform changes and follicular atrophoderma
Screen for and surgically treat cataracts, which are often asymmetric or sectorial, through ophthalmology
Monitor and manage the skeletal features — scoliosis and asymmetric limb shortening — with orthopaedic surveillance and intervention as needed
Confirm the diagnosis with plasma sterol analysis and EBP molecular testing, capturing stippled epiphyses on infant radiographs before they resolve
Coordinate care through a multidisciplinary team of clinical genetics, dermatology, ophthalmology and orthopaedics
Offer genetic counselling explaining the X-linked dominant inheritance, female predominance and male lethality, with family screening
